If there's a moment that best embodies the clash between reason and emotion in Apple's technology, it was yesterday's new iPhone launch event.

I watched the iPhone Duo portion of yesterday's keynote in the morning and couldn't help but drool all over my desk, but for me, the true stars of yesterday's event were the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, all because of their brand new camera features……

Variable aperture—with a caveat

Considering the supply chain required to introduce a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it's no surprise that this feature was thoroughly leaked before the launch. The only thing that wasn't entirely clear was whether this feature would be available on both iPhone Pro models, or limited to the Pro Max only. The good news is it's the former.

Apple also confirmed that while the iPhone will automatically adjust the aperture in certain situations, we can also have full manual control. I mentioned beforehand that expectations may need to be tempered regarding the practical differences this feature brings.

But I also speculated whether Apple would enhance Portrait mode this time, using the combination of a larger aperture and computational photography to produce results better than hardware alone could achieve. This remains to be verified, but judging from some of the sample photos shown, I do feel my speculation was correct.

I will personally test this feature and, of course, share the results with everyone.

Low-light photography and videography

The maximum aperture is also nearly a full stop brighter than the previous generation, going from the iPhone 17 Pro's f/1.78 to f/1.48. While this may not make a huge difference to depth of field itself, it should be a fairly decent improvement for shooting in low-light environments (including night scenes).

Manual shutter speed control

In addition to manually controlling the aperture, we can also select shutter speed for photos and videos.

For photos, this means being able to shoot long exposures. The promotional video demonstrated how to use this feature to create motion blur effects. We still don't know what the maximum exposure time can reach, nor whether the combination of the narrowest aperture and computational techniques can achieve a 30-second exposure—a commonly used technique that can render flowing water silky smooth. The same technique can also be used to make pedestrians "disappear" from the frame.

With traditional cameras, achieving this effect requires a neutral density filter (ND filter) to reduce the amount of light entering, but there are third-party iPhone apps on the market that can combine a series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar effect. I personally often use the Spectre app to do this.

For video, manual shutter speed control allows me to apply the 180-degree shutter rule. When shooting at 24 fps, setting the shutter speed to 1/48 second yields the most natural motion blur. Although we could already do this in third-party professional shooting apps like Blackmagic Cam, it's even better now that Apple's built-in app has the same functionality.

White balance control

Another feature previously found only in third-party apps is white balance control, which has now also been added to the built-in app.

For photography, this allows us to adjust colour temperature according to our own taste, but it's even more important for videography. Automatic white balance means the colour temperature, and the overall feel of the image, may continuously shift throughout a clip, creating an obvious amateurish look. Being able to lock the white balance throughout the entire recording process is a significant improvement.

Cinematic Mode for all video

Cinematic Mode is the video version of Portrait mode, allowing us to add artificial shallow depth of field effects. All along, we've had to choose between standard video and Cinematic Mode—even though the latter actually still outputs a flat video. With the iPhone 18 Pro, we can shoot standard video first and then decide whether to add the Cinematic Mode effect afterwards.

In addition, we can now shoot Cinematic Mode video at up to 60 fps, allowing it to be used for capturing slow-motion footage.

Intelligent video focus mode

Current iPhones already allow you to set focus tracking on a specific person in the frame, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a more advanced version.

Specifically, it seems to use artificial intelligence to identify specific people, maintaining stable tracking of the subject even when others walk across in front of the lens. Even if the subject leaves the frame and re-enters, it will re-lock onto them.

Histogram

This feature had been rumoured well before yesterday's keynote, so I'll just briefly recap what was said at the time.

Battery life

Video shooting is very power-hungry, so improvements in this area are good news. We don't have specific figures for this use case, but since the Pro Max's maximum usage time has increased from 39 hours to 45 hours, it's estimated that shooting time will be roughly 15% longer than last year's model.

Apple-certified original image reference

Lastly, there is a way to prove the authenticity of photos when needed. This is clearly a professional tool, most relevant to roles such as news photographers and law enforcement.

Summary

Of course, some people's eyes will only be on the iPhone Duo, which is completely understandable. But if your iPhone is an important part of your camera kit, then the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the real winners this time.
